Storytelling and Transformation: Narratives of Self from Homer to Ariana Huffington. This course explores storytelling and its junctures with the idea of self from the past to the present. We trace the beginnings of this phenomenon in the Odyssey and see its evolution through time in Europe and Modern Greece to end the course with a discussion about the role of storytelling in entrepreneurial culture in the United States today. Students become acquainted with important concepts, topics, and terms in the classical tradition and reception and develop their own definitions as they engage in conversation about modern contexts.

title: Exploring the Greek and Roman World

sections.note: How to Read and Write like Cleopatra. This class introduces the technology of reading and writing available in the lifetime of Cleopatra, and also the most common educational practices of that time. Students will learn to make and use several of the writing media that were dominant before the printing press (wax tablets, clay tablets, papyrus paper, ink), and they will see how people approached learning to read and write when skills like memory and improvisation were integral to the process. The main focus will be Egypt in the 1st century BCE, but related places and times will be discussed.

"Fish Sauce, Sparrows, and Pancakes: Food in the Roman World". Today, the ancient Romans are notorious for lavish dining, however, in their own time many regarded plain bean and grain porridge as the Roman national dish. Sometimes this was an insult made by Rome's sophisticated Greek neighbors, while at others it was an evocation of the most fundamental forms of Roman identity and virtue. Modern anthropologists often consider practices around food, cooking, and eating as fundamental ways of understanding a culture. This class will take the culinary world of the ancient Romans as a way of understanding a wide range of topics around ancient Rome, including agriculture, food supply, religion, social interaction, class, and taste. Together we will engage with original Roman writings about food, modern scholarship, and bring many surviving Roman recipes to life to taste ourselves and share with the campus community.

Wonders of the Ancient World. In this class you will study the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World: the Great Pyramid of Giza, Hanging Gardens of Babylon, Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, Statue of Zeus at Olympia, Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, Colossus of Rhodes, and the Lighthouse of Alexandria. You will learn how they were made, what they meant to the people who built them, and the ways they have influenced modern art and architecture. Field trips to architectural wonders on the UIUC campus will enrich our understanding of the past.

Nightmares of Nero. Few Roman emperors have been so constantly reviled in history and popular culture as Nero. Ancient sources depict him as a deviant, a larger-than-life monster, a tyrant, a megalomaniac, an arsonist, a murderer. Early Christians demonized him as their greatest persecutor, and apocalyptic prophecies identified him with the Antichrist. Setting its sights on the various myths and exaggerations that have come down to us about Nero, this course explores the question of what we can know of the infamous emperor and the age that bears his name. Particular emphasis will be placed on the nightmarish refractions of Neronian Rome found in the works of Seneca, Lucan, and Petronius.

Pompeii: Life in a Roman City. Pompeii, a city in the Bay of Naples famously destroyed but uniquely preserved by the eruption of Mt. Vesuvius in 79 CE, has traditionally been viewed as the quintessential example of the ancient Roman urban experience. But just how ‘Roman’ was Pompeii? This class examines how evidence from Pompeii contributes to our knowledge of Roman material culture and the everyday use of urban space; and questions whether our broader conception of Roman life is limited by our reliance on evidence from this one city. In answering such questions, we will deepen our understanding of what it meant to be Roman in the ancient Mediterranean world.

Thinking about Trauma through Athenian Drama - Ancient theater offered the space for reflecting upon the violence and trauma for its original audiences and for contemporary societies. This course focuses on the experiences of the ancients with war, trauma, and the plight of veterans, prisoners of war, and refugees. It also looks beyond Athenian theater to modern adaptations by theater companies, playwrights, directors and speaks to modern issues, making the plays respond to the ravages of contemporary wars, the experience of refugees, and gender violence: allowing them to speak directly to communities of color and issues of social justice. Readings include both ancient Greek plays and modern adaptations of select plays. This CLCV 220 will be co-taught by Paul O'Mahony, Director of Out-of-Chaos Theatre, London, UK and in the second half of the semester students will work with Paul O'Mahony, Kim McKean (Theater) and Angeliki Tzanetou (Classics) in writing and performing an adaptation of Aeschylus's Suppliants.
